abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: The goal of this clinical trial is to test if the drug SKY-0515, an oral medication, can lower harmful proteins linked to Huntington's Disease (HD) and improve the symptoms of participants with HD. This study includes men and women aged 25 and older who have HD confirmed by genetic testing and meet certain requirements for physical ability and independence.
description: This study is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted across multiple sites. This clinical trial aims to evaluate the safety, pharmacodynamics, and efficacy of SKY-0515, a novel, orally administered small molecule. Huntington's Disease (HD) is a rare, inherited neurodegenerative condition caused by a mutation in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, resulting in excessive production of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein, which damages nerve cells and leads to progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. SKY-0515 is designed to reduce mHTT protein levels, leading to a decrease in both wild-type and mutant forms of HTT protein. Additionally, the drug lowers postmeiotic segregation 1 (PMS1) protein, which plays a role in somatic CAG repeat expansion-a key driver of HD progression. Participants must be aged 25 or older, have genetically confirmed HD (CAG repeat length ≥ 40), and meet specific functional and motor criteria. They will be assigned randomly to one of four treatment arms (three doses of SKY-0515 and one placebo group). Safety and efficacy will be evaluated through blood tests, imaging (MRI), and clinical assessments, including the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (UHDRS).

outcomes.description: cUHDRS includes the Total Functional Capacity (range, 0-13; higher score means better functioning), Total Motor Score (range, 0-124; higher score means worse motor severity), Symbol Digit Modality Test (range, 0-110, correctly paired numbers-symbols in 90 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance), and Stroop Color and Word Test (range, 0-no max value, correctly read color words in 45 seconds; higher score means better cognitive performance) scores. A z-score for each test is calculated, which alone can be used to describe relationship between an individual's test score and the mean score of a target population. A z-score of 0 is the mean, and ±1 is 1 standard deviation from the mean. For cUHDRS, z-scores of each test are summed, whereby a higher cUHDRS score is better (score of -3.06-no max value) and a change of ≥1.2 is a meaningful worsening, shown to track functional decline.
outcomes.measure: Change From Baseline in the Z-score from the Composite Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale (cUHDRS)

outcomes.description: The total motor score (TMS) assessed motor features of HD with standardized ratings of oculomotor function, dysarthria, chorea, dystonia, gait, and postural stability. Some items (such as chorea and dystonia) required grading each extremity (face, bucco-oral-lingual, and trunk) separately. Eye movements require both horizontal and vertical grades. The total motor impairment score is the sum of all the individual 31 motor sub-items (each rated from 0 to 4), with higher scores indicating more severe motor impairment than lower scores. The range of TMS is 0-124.
outcomes.measure: Change from Baseline in Total Motor Score (TMS)

abstract: The aim of the study is to decipher the alterations in signalling pathways of skeletal muscle stem cells (satellite cells (SCs)) in individuals with COPD, as well as to examine the effect of exercise training on SCs. To this end, the team will perform an exhaustive evaluation of lung and muscle function, including exercise capacity, as well as muscle biopsies, before and after a 2-months rehabilitation program. This study should provide new therapeutic avenues for COPD-associated sarcopenia.
description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is now to be considered as a multimorbid disease, originating from a combination of several risk factors (respiratory events in childhood, exposure to inhaled particles, physical inactivity, etc.), and simultaneously affecting several organs. This multi-organ impairment is likely to arise from common biological processes such as systemic inflammation or repair failure. Studying these processes in an organ that is easily accessible to biopsy, such as skeletal muscle, can help in the overall management of COPD. Skeletal muscle wasting (or sarcopenia: loss of muscle mass and force) is also a major comorbidity in COPD, both frequent and associated to increased mortality. Muscle stem cells (satellite cells) are responsible for repairing skeletal muscle tissue after injury, notably after micro-lesions induced by exercise. However, they have been scarcely studied in COPD. In the present project, the team proposes to study repair abnormalities in skeletal muscle tissue by comparing the signalling pathways activated in satellite cells of patients with COPD, before and after a respiratory rehabilitation programme (20 sessions over 8 to 12 weeks). The team will carry out an exhaustive respiratory and muscular assessment at inclusion and at the end of the 20 sessions, evaluating in particular respiratory function and exercise capacity (Pulmonary Function Tests, cardio-pulmonary exercise testing with VO2max measurement, 6-minute walking test, handgrip test) as well as a quadricipital muscle biopsy with the modified Bergström's technique. Muscle biopsies will be used to culture satellite cells and assess their regenerative capacity in vitro, as well as to analyse dysregulated signalling pathways at the transcriptomic level with single-cell RNAsequencing. The results should help to identify new therapeutic avenues for the comprehensive management of multimorbid COPD.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Hypertension remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet blood pressure control rates remain suboptimal despite the widespread availability of effective antihypertensive therapies. Poor long-term adherence, therapeutic inertia, and the need for lifelong daily treatment continue to limit the effectiveness of current pharmacological strategies. This review examines the biological rationale, available clinical evidence, and potential role of long-acting RNA-based therapies targeting hepatic angiotensinogen synthesis in hypertension.
RECENT FINDINGS: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting angiotensinogen represent a novel therapeutic approach that suppresses production of the unique precursor of the renin-angiotensin system. Zilebesiran has demonstrated sustained reductions in circulating angiotensinogen and ambulatory blood pressure following infrequent subcutaneous administration in phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials. Antisense strategies have provided additional clinical validation of sustained angiotensinogen inhibition, although their antihypertensive efficacy has been less consistent. Ongoing clinical development is addressing long-term cardiovascular outcomes, safety, and optimal patient selection. RNA-based antihypertensive therapies may represent an important evolution in hypertension management by combining upstream renin-angiotensin system inhibition with prolonged pharmacological activity and reduced dependence on daily medication adherence. However, their future clinical role will depend on evidence regarding long-term safety, cardiovascular outcomes, reversibility, cost-effectiveness, patient selection, and integration with conventional antihypertensive therapy.

abstract:
PURPOSE: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is important in promoting a pro-oncogenic tumor microenvironment. This first randomized trial of a STAT3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide with pembrolizumab assessed whether this first-line combination would improve outcomes compared with pembrolizumab alone in recurrent/metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label, controlled study (NCT05814666) enrolled patients with previously untreated R/M HNSCC with positive PD-L1 expression [combined positive score (CPS) ≥1]. Patients were stratified by CPS (1-19; ≥20) and randomized 2:1 to danvatirsen 3 mg/kg intravenously weekly (with two loading doses in week 1) plus pembrolizumab 200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks or pembrolizumab alone. Patients received 21-day treatment cycles until progressive disease, unacceptable toxicity, or voluntary withdrawal. Primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR; partial + complete response per RECIST v1.1).
RESULTS: Sixty-nine patients were randomized, and 66 were treated [51 (77.3%) male]: 45 with danvatirsen + pembrolizumab and 21 with pembrolizumab alone. Enrollment was stopped due to lack of response in the CPS 1 to 19 cohort after ≥1 scan (∼6 weeks of treatment) and in the CPS ≥20 cohort after ≥2 scans (∼12 weeks). In the final analysis, ORRs were 15.6% and 14.3%, respectively (risk difference 1.3; P = 1). The treatment-emergent adverse event rate was increased in the combination arm (97.8% vs. 85.7%), and the combination side effect profile was similar to previous danvatirsen studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Combination danvatirsen + pembrolizumab did not improve ORR compared with pembrolizumab alone in first-line treatment of R/M HNSCC. Further exploration of STAT3-targeted approaches is needed within the context of immunotherapy.

title: Danvatirsen plus Pembrolizumab versus Pembrolizumab for Recurrent and/or Metastatic Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (PEMDA-HN): A Randomized, Phase II Trial.

abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics (NATs), including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics and programmable editing technologies, are reshaping the therapeutic landscape for inherited metabolic and genetic disease. Unlike conventional small molecules or biologics, NATs enable sequence-directed modulation of target gene expression and therefore provide unprecedented flexibility for targeting pathogenic mechanisms previously considered undruggable. Recent clinical successes have established proof of concept for multiple NAT modalities across neurological, hepatic, muscular and metabolic disorders. However, broader implementation remains constrained by challenges in tissue-specific delivery, biomarker validation, natural-history infrastructure and evidence generation in ultra-rare populations. In parallel, increasing platform reproducibility is beginning to challenge traditional product-based regulatory paradigms. This review examines the principal classes of NATs and proposes a practical framework for modality selection based on disease biology, tissue accessibility, durability, reversibility and clinical context. We discuss key translational bottlenecks beyond delivery, including biomarker-outcome relationships, small-population trial design and the limitations of conventional evidentiary frameworks in rare disease. A central theme of this review is the growing transition from isolated precision medicines towards increasingly programmable therapeutic platforms. We explore how advances in extrahepatic delivery, computational oligonucleotide design, artificial intelligence-assisted optimisation and programmable editing technologies may progressively support more scalable and individualised therapeutic development. Finally, we discuss emerging regulatory frameworks that may better accommodate platform-level predictability while maintaining rigorous evaluation of sequence-specific and disease-specific risks.

title: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Rare Disease: From Precision Medicine to Programmable Platforms.

abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuroinflammation is a characteristic feature of many neurological diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes results in the production of proinflammatory mediators that contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration.
PURPOSE: CRISPR/Cas9 genome-editing technology provides highly precise targeting of genes involved in these pathways, enabling the deletion, correction, or modulation of disease-associated genetic alterations. Nonetheless, effective delivery of CRISPR components to the central nervous system (CNS) remains a major challenge because of protective barriers such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB), as well as concerns regarding genomic instability and immunogenicity.
METHODS: Nanotechnology-guided delivery platforms, such as lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, dendrimers and polymeric carriers, have been developed as promising strategies to address these challenges. These nanosystems can improve biodistribution, pharmacokinetic behavior, and cellular uptake, while potentially reducing off-target effects and systemic toxicity.
RESULTS: The preclinical studies demonstrate successful modulation of key neuroinflammatory targets, including the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2), Janus kinase (JAK) signaling, and the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway, with potential therapeutic relevance to neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, novel techniques, such as mitochondrial base editing, prime editing, and epigenetic modulation, expand the scope of CRISPR-mediated therapeutic strategies. Although outcomes from animal models are promising, translation to the clinical setting requires careful consideration of safety, ethical concerns, and long-term efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: This review highlights the potential of integrating CRISPR/Cas9 with nanodelivery systems to advance precision medicine for neuroinflammatory disorders, while emphasizing their potential for therapeutic applications in complex CNS conditions. Ongoing studies aimed at optimizing delivery and reducing off-target effects will be essential for advancing these approaches toward clinical practice.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-based nanodelivery systems for precision gene editing in neuroinflammation.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is prone to relapse driven by therapy-persistent residual cells. To discover specific vulnerabilities in this population, we performed genome-wide CRISPR interference screens in leukemia cells treated with multiple agents. KHSRP was the top hit, the depletion of which sensitized AML cells to therapy and substantially prolonged survival in treated AML-bearing mice. Analysis of in vivo residual disease after venetoclax/azacitidine treatment identified downregulation of the vitamin C and uric acid transporter SLC23A1, which mediated resistance to multiple therapies. KHSRP depletion restored SLC23A1 expression by preventing its ZC3H4-mediated nuclear mRNA degradation. KHSRP depletion therefore enhanced the synergistic cytotoxicity of vitamin C and uric acid, particularly in therapy-persistent leukemia cells. Re-expression of TET2 overrode the chemosensitizing effect of KHSRP depletion in TET2-mutant leukemia, suggesting that KHSRP-linked phenotypes were related to vitamin C- and uric acid-mediated TET activation. These findings suggest targeting KHSRP to enhance treatment efficacy and selectively eradicate residual AML.
SIGNIFICANCE: Residual AML cells that persist following therapy have distinct biological properties compared with initial disease or overt relapse. Here, we nominate KHSRP as a target to improve therapy efficacy and exploit selective vulnerabilities of AML residual disease.

title: Therapy-Persistent Leukemia Is Selectively Vulnerable to SLC23A1 Restoration via Targeting KHSRP.

abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics (ONTs) have revolutionized the medical landscape by enabling the precise modulation of genetic pathways. This perspective highlights the major conjugation strategies for ONTs, using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) as representative modalities. We describe diverse classes of targeting ligands, including small molecules, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), antibodies, and aptamers. For example, triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) conjugation has enabled a number of approved oligonucleotide therapeutics. Meanwhile, other emerging conjugation technologies have expanded oligonucleotide delivery to extrahepatic tissues to address a broader range of diseases. We further summarize the clinical translation of these delivery platforms, highlighting approved therapeutics alongside emerging clinical candidates. Finally, we provide an outlook on challenges and opportunities for the next generation of oligonucleotide therapeutics.

title: Advances in therapeutic oligonucleotide conjugates.

abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.
RECENT FINDINGS: Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

abstract: Stargardt disease is caused by biallelic variants in the ABCA4 gene and is the most frequent autosomal recessive macular degeneration in childhood and adolescence. No approved disease-modifying treatment has yet been approved. The size of the ABCA4 gene represents a challenge for conventional gene therapy based on adeno-associated viruses (AAV) and was the stimulus for the development of innovative strategies. Gene supplementation therapies use lentiviral or dual AAV vectors to introduce complete copies of the healthy ABCA4 gene into the target cells, whereas gene editing procedures, such as RNA exon editing or base editing, enable direct correction of the mutations causing the diseases. Intravitreal injection of antisense oligonucleotides selectively addresses splicing defects and provides a less invasive intravitreal approach but requires repeated applications. Indirect therapies modulate the visual cycle or neuroprotective signalling pathways and can be applied independent of variants. Finally, disease-agnostic approaches, such as optogenetics, enable restoration of vision in cases of advanced degeneration by the use of preserved inner retinal layers. The diversity of these approaches takes account of the broad spectrum of diseases that ranges from a disease limited to the macula to a generalized rod-cone dystrophy and perspectively opens up individualized treatment strategies depending on the genotype and phenotype.

title: [Genetic therapies for Stargardt disease].

abstract: ATP1A3-related neurological disorders comprise a rapidly expanding spectrum of rare neurogenetic diseases characterized by remarkable clinical heterogeneity and complex genotype-phenotype relationships. Since the publication of previous comprehensive reviews, the identification of novel ATP1A3-associated phenotypes, refinement of genotype-phenotype correlations, and advances in molecular pathogenesis and precision therapeutic strategies have substantially expanded current understanding of these disorders, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis. This narrative review summarizes recent advances in the clinical spectrum of ATP1A3-related disorders and discusses current insights into genotype-phenotype correlations, molecular mechanisms, and disease pathogenesis. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular consequences of ATP1A3 dysfunction, including impaired Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, disrupted neuronal excitability, altered ion homeostasis, and downstream cellular responses. We further review current symptomatic management and emerging disease-modifying therapeutic strategies, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, viral vector-mediated gene delivery, genome editing technologies, and other precision medicine approaches. Current challenges and future research priorities are also discussed. By integrating recent clinical and experimental evidence, this review provides an updated perspective on ATP1A3-related disorders and aims to facilitate improved disease recognition, mechanistic understanding, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

abstract: β-Thalassemia, a major genetic disease affecting the global population, has seen new strategies being pursued in terms of curative attempts directed at the specific gene defect present. Iron chelation therapy and lifelong blood transfusions have historically been used to treat β-thalassemia, a severe hereditary hemoglobin condition marked by decreased or missing β-globin chain synthesis. These methods have significantly increased patient survival, but they do not offer a permanent solution and are linked to serious side effects and a high cost of care. With a focus on hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), lentiviral gene-addition treatment, and future genome-editing techniques, this study outlines new and creative methods to long-term disease correction in β-thalassemia. Although allogeneic HSCT is still a proven treatment option, its use is constrained by the availability of donors, graft-related issues, and transplant-related hazards. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell-based gene therapy has become a significant substitute, provided the possibility of long-term transfusion independence while prevented graft-versus-host disease. With the creation of exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel; Casgevy), which reactivates fetal hemoglobin expression through modification of the BCL11A erythroid enhancer and has shown significant rates of sustained transfusion independence in eligible patients with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has recently marked a significant clinical milestone. Notwithstanding these encouraging developments, myeloablative conditioning, long-term safety and durability, high treatment costs, complicated manufacturing requirements, and restricted accessibility continue to be major obstacles, especially in low- and middle-income nations. All things considered, the therapeutic landscape for β-thalassemia is changing from lifelong supportive management to potentially curative and transformative interventions; however, the wider application of these cutting-edge therapies depends on ongoing long-term evaluation and efforts to increase affordability and global accessibility.

title: Recent trends and innovative strategies in the curative approach for β-thalassemia: a current prospect and future perspective.

abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

abstract: Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has emerged as an important cancer dependency and suppressor of innate immunity. While early therapeutic strategies focused on global enzymatic inhibition, these approaches may compromise essential homeostatic functions of the constitutively expressed ADAR1-p110 isoform. Growing evidence highlights editing-independent functions uniquely mediated by the interferon-inducible ADAR1-p150 isoform. Through its conformation-specific Zα domain, ADAR1-p150 binds Z-nucleic acids and suppresses MDA5-, PKR-, and ZBP1-driven innate immune activation, thereby promoting tumor immune evasion and adaptation to inflammatory stress. Consequently, selectively disrupting this p150-mediated suppression may represent a more therapeutically tractable strategy than global ADAR1 inhibition, with the Zα domain providing a potentially selective mechanistic interface. This review synthesizes current understanding of Zα-mediated immune regulation, evaluates emerging domain-specific therapeutic approaches, and provides a comprehensive guide to the biophysical and cell-based assays used to interrogate Zα interactions, highlighting key mechanistic gaps that may inform future p150-selective translational interventions.

title: The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target.

abstract: Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.

abstract: Respiratory diseases remain major causes of morbidity and mortality; however, inadequate pulmonary drug exposure and systemic toxicity continue to limit treatment efficacy. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities for localized, sustained, and targeted therapy. This review examines how disease biology informs pulmonary delivery design across pulmonary fibrosis, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary infections, and acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. It outlines anatomical and biological barriers and compares liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric and hybrid systems, biomimetic carriers, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Particular attention is given to matching therapeutic cargo and carrier properties to fibroblasts, macrophages, tumor cells, and alveolar type II cells. Emerging approaches include mRNA delivery, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR-based editing, alongside alveolar regeneration and biomarker-guided treatment. These strategies are evaluated in relation to their delivery requirements and stage of development. The review also addresses aerosol-device compatibility, manufacturing, repeated-dose safety, regulatory considerations, and clinical outcomes. By connecting delivery mechanisms with disease-specific applications and clinical evidence, this review identifies both therapeutic opportunities and barriers to translation. This integrated perspective can guide the development of inhaled nanomedicines with more reproducible pulmonary delivery, improved treatment efficacy, and acceptable safety.

abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

abstract:
PURPOSE: MEDI1191 is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated messenger RNA (mRNA) designed to induce local interleukin (IL) 12 production and intensify antitumor T-cell responses. We report dose-escalation results from a first-in-human, open-label, phase I study of intratumoral MEDI1191 plus intravenous durvalumab (NCT03946800).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients were ≥18 years with advanced/metastatic solid tumors and had progressed on ≥1 line of prior therapy (immunotherapy permitted). Cutaneous/subcutaneous (parts 1A and 1B) or deep-seated lesions (part 1D) were injected; patients had ≥1 noninjected lesion measurable per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1). Target lesions were noninjected. MEDI1191 and durvalumab were given sequentially (part 1A) or concurrently (parts 1B and 1D). Primary objectives were safety and determination of maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included efficacy.
RESULTS: As of February 27, 2023, 61 patients were treated. Patients had a median of four prior regimens (range, 1-17); 39 (63.9%) received prior anti-programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) occurred in 96.7% of patients, and 41.0% experienced grade 3/4 TEAEs. There were no dose-limiting toxicities. The MTD was not reached. The objective response rate was 9.8%, including 1 confirmed complete response and 5 confirmed partial responses (PR). The duration of response was 2.7 to 22.3 months; the median was not reached. Responses occurred in injected lesions, local noninjected lesions, and distant lesions. Three of the 39 patients with prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy had PRs.
CONCLUSIONS: MEDI1191 and durvalumab were tolerated. Preliminary antitumor activity was encouraging in these heavily pretreated patients, including patients previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.

abstract: Noncoding RNAs have recently emerged as promising targets for therapeutic drugs. However, their high conformational flexibility presents significant challenges in structure-based rational drug discovery. Therefore, it is essential to gain detailed mechanistic insights into the millisecond-time scale ligand recognition process coupled to RNA conformational dynamics. Enhanced sampling simulations can help investigate these intricate dynamical processes by effectively exploring the rugged conformational landscapes of RNA-ligand complexes. In this study, we applied the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling algorithm and its flooding variant to compute the free energy surface, kinetics, and binding mechanism for three different natural and synthetic ligands to a prototypical RNA aptamer. Our simulations revealed the dynamic coupling between ligand recognition and the base-flipping transition. In addition to reproducing the relative trends of binding affinities and residence times, our results uncovered a competing effect between the conformational selection and the induced fit mechanisms. The preference for one mechanism over the other is influenced by the binding affinity. By integrating these mechanistic insights with the binding affinity and kinetics derived from our simulations, we provide an atomistically detailed understanding of the RNA-ligand recognition process.

abstract: The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPRassociated protein 9 (Cas9) system has revolutionized genome editing through its precision, simplicity, and programmability. The clinical translation of CRISPR/Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains constrained by major delivery challenges, including large molecular size, instability in biological fluids, and limited cellular penetration. Nanoparticle-mediated, non-viral delivery systems have emerged as a compelling strategy to overcome these barriers by providing targeted, transient, and biocompatible transport of Cas9 RNPs into cells. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in lipid-based, polymeric, peptide, and exosome-derived nanocarriers, focusing on their design principles, mechanisms of uptake, and endosomal escape strategies. Particular attention is given to receptor-mediated targeting, intracellular trafficking, and the emerging translation of lipid nanoparticle systems such as NTLA-2001, which exemplify clinical progress in genome editing. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist. Nanoparticle systems exhibit trade-offs between efficiency, biocompatibility, and scalability. For example, lipid nanoparticles may trigger anti- PEG immune reactions, exosome production faces manufacturing constraints, and polymeric systems risk cytotoxicity or limited degradability. Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 proteins and unpredictable immune responses to nanoparticle components remain significant translational hurdles. By integrating current preclinical and early clinical evidence, this review highlights both the promise and the limitations of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 RNP delivery. Understanding these biological, immunological, and engineering challenges will be crucial for developing safe, efficient, and clinically scalable genome editing platforms.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 Rnps Into Cells.

abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

abstract: The clinical validation of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines in 2020-2021 accelerated the development of synthetic messenger RNA as a precision therapeutic platform beyond infectious disease prevention. Unlike gene therapy approaches that permanently modify genomic DNA, synthetic mRNA enables transient protein expression through programmable molecular engineering. This narrative review examines therapeutic applications of engineered mRNA, emphasizing its epigenomic potential. It discusses key engineering strategies, including nucleoside modifications, codon optimization, untranslated region engineering, cap chemistry, and advances in lipid nanoparticle and alternative delivery systems. Six therapeutic domains are explored: cancer immunotherapy, cardiac regeneration, monogenic diseases, genome and epigenome editing, autoimmune disease, and somatic cell reprogramming. Particular attention is given to mRNA-mediated replacement of chromatin regulators, dCas9-based epigenome editing, epigenetically derived tumor antigens, and transcription-factor-driven cellular reprogramming. The review distinguishes chemical nucleoside modifications from endogenous epitranscriptomic regulation and examines the differences between transient protein expression, heritable but reversible chromatin changes, and permanent genomic modifications. Clinical evidence, discontinued programs, and preclinical developments are critically evaluated. Despite promising advances, major challenges remain regarding delivery specificity, durability, safety, and clinical translation. Overall, synthetic mRNA represents an emerging platform for molecular and epigenetic therapeutic reprogramming beyond vaccination.

abstract: CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing represents a paradigm shift from static DNA sequence editing to dynamic reprogramming of gene expression, offering a powerful and precise toolbox with the potential to develop stable and climate-resilient crops without altering DNA sequences. The escalating challenges of global food security, driven by climate change and population growth, necessitate innovative crop improvement strategies that extend beyond conventional breeding. Although CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionized plant biotechnology through direct genome editing, CRISPR-based epigenome editing has emerged as a new frontier. By repurposing nuclease-dead Cas9 as a programmable targeting platform fused to epigenetic effector domains, researchers can precisely modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. This approach has already yielded compelling successes, such as the engineering of durable resistance to cassava bacterial blight through targeted epigenetic silencing of a susceptibility gene. This review focuses primarily on the current state of CRISPR-based epigenome editing systems, including acetyltransferases, demethylases, DNA methyltransferases, and deacetylases, and their applications in crop improvement research. We critically evaluate their mechanisms in rewriting epigenetic regulatory information, their demonstrated efficacy in enhancing yield components, disease resistance, and abiotic stress tolerance, and their potential to create stable meiotically heritable epialleles, although most demonstrations remain at the proof-of-concept stage in model plants, with field validation in major crops still limited. This review provides a balanced analysis of key challenges, including editing specificity, context-dependency, delivery limitations, and regulatory considerations. Finally, we outline future directions focusing on technological refinement, multi-omics integration, and field validation. Epigenome editing shows promise as a conceptually distinct and transformative approach in crop biotechnology, through targeted modulation of a plant's epigenetic landscape. However, its full potential hinges on overcoming challenges related to stability, predictability, and field-scale validation.

abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

abstract: Genome-targeting strategies to address NaV1.7-mediated signaling in nociceptive afferents are of great clinical interest given its high selectivity and persistent analgesic outcomes. In the present work, we analyze concentration-dependent effects of suppressing primary afferent NaV1.7 using the intrathecal delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) on pain behaviors and demonstrate that NaV1.7 ASOs are likely to modulate pain traffic by blocking afferent signaling at the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) level. Intrathecal NaV1.7 ASOs induced a concentration-dependent gradient of knockdown in DRGs (lumbar to cervical) of Scn9a mRNA and ATTO488-ProTx-II binding in small DRG neurons, and a suppression of pain behaviors initiated by mechanical compression, inflammation, and the NaV1.7 agonist OD-1. The rostro-caudal reduction in mRNA correlated with ASO distribution, with implications for dose-related analgesic profiles. Marked reduction in DRG NaV1.7 binding was seen after intrathecal delivery of an ASO optimal dose, with high selectivity for small DRG neurons. Changes in sciatic nerve NaV1.7 binding were not detected, indicating a pain traffic modulation likely happening due to a block of afferent signaling at the DRG level.

abstract: Anisomeles indica (L.) Kuntze is an important traditional medicinal plant with diverse pharmacological activities, while no mitochondrial genome (mitogenome) has yet been reported for this species or any member of the genus, limiting our understanding of organelle genome evolution and molecular characteristics within Lamiaceae. In this study, we report the first complete mitogenome of the genus Anisomeles, which was de novo assembled and annotated for A. indica using PacBio high-fidelity (HiFi) sequencing data. The mitogenome of A. indica was assembled as a single master circular molecule with a length of 296,457 bp and a GC content of 45.42%. A total of 51 genes were identified, including 32 protein-coding genes (PCGs), three rRNA genes and 16 tRNA genes. Repeat analysis revealed relatively low repeat abundance, with 60 simple sequence repeats, 136 dispersed repeats, and 15 tandem repeats identified. Furthermore, 30 mitochondrial plastid DNA sequences were detected (24,696 bp), suggesting a substantial contribution of plastid-derived sequences to the mitogenome. RNA editing analysis predicted 444 editing sites across all mitochondrial PCGs except atp1. Phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial and plastid genome datasets supported a closer relationship of A. indica with Pogostemon than with Phlomoides. This study provides the first mitogenomic resource for Anisomeles and establishes a foundation for future studies of mitogenome evolution, comparative genomics, and phylogenetic relationships within Lamiaceae.

abstract:
Background:

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare immune disorder caused by a mutation in the CYBB gene. People with CGD have white blood cells that do not work properly and are at greater risk of getting infections. Researchers want to know if gene therapy using the patient's own base-edited stem cells can improve the white cells' functioning and result in fewer CGD-related infections.

Objective:

To learn if base-edited stem cells will correct the white blood cells in people with CGD.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18 years and older with X-linked CGD.

Design:

This is a non-randomized study. Participants with the specific mutation under study will be screened during the initial phase.

During the development phase, participants will undergo apheresis to collect stem cells for base-editing correction of the mutation.

During the treatment phase, participants will first receive Campath (alemtuzumab) to reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells. This will be followed by conditioning chemotherapy with busulfan and subsequent infusion of the base-edited stem cells. Participants will be maintained on sirolimus to further reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells.

Follow-up visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

Open-label, phase 1/2 trial to determine the safety, and efficacy of a single infusion of base-edited (BE) autologous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) for treatment of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD). Base editing is performed to repair CYBB missense gene mutations (eg, CYBB c.676C\>T). The study hypotheses are that 1) base editing can efficiently repair gene mutations in HSPCs; and 2) BE HSPCs can engraft and differentiate into functional phagocytes with restored nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase activity.

During the initial development phase each study participant will undergo apheresis for CD34+ HSPC collection for the development and validation of a mutation-specific BE system.

During the treatment phase, participants will receive a one-time infusion of the BE autologous HSPC (study product) after the administration of Campath (alemtuzumab) and of busulfan conditioning (total 12 mg/kg with a targeted total AUC of 65,000 ng/mL x hr). Sirolimus will be initiated on Day -1 and may be given for approximately 3-6 months.

Participants will have follow-up evaluations at months 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24, and yearly thereafter until 5 years after treatment. Key study assessments include adverse event (AE) assessment, blood laboratory evaluations of functional protein made from the target gene (CYBB, encodes for gp91\^phox), and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing to identify rates of gene repair and off-target mutation.

The final study follow-up under this protocol will be at 5 years, but long-term follow-up under a separate NIH protocol will continue annually to 15 years after treatment.

Objectives:

Primary Objectives:

* To evaluate the safety of BE autologous CD34+ cells.
* To evaluate the efficacy of BE autologous CD34+ cells.

Secondary Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Efficiency of base editing (percentages of target nucleotide conversion).
* Engraftment capability of BE HSPCs.
* Efficiency in restoring gp91\^phox expression
* Efficiency in restoring NADPH oxidase function.
* Clinical efficacy.
* Stability of gene correction.

Exploratory Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Specificity of base editing by assessing rates of off-target edits at top predicted sites.
* Random off-target edits by whole genome sequencing (WGS).

Endpoints:

Primary Endpoints:

* Safety of gene therapy using BE autologous HSPCs as measured by study product-related AEs and serious AEs (SAEs) through 2 years after treatment.
* Efficacy of gene therapy determined as percentages of subjects who have \>= 10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months after infusion.

Secondary Endpoints:

* Determine frequency of converted target nucleotide alleles.
* Assess the frequency of gene-modified alleles compared to infusion product in peripheral blood at 12 months.
* Evaluate efficacy of restoring gp91\^phox expression.
* Evaluate efficacy of NADPH oxidase functional restoration as measured by the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry oxidase assay at 12 months after treatment (\>=10% oxidase-positive neutrophils), or by quantitative measurement of reactive oxygen species (ROS) using the ferricytochrome C assay on peripheral blood granulocytes.
* Evaluate clinical benefit by improvement of baseline clinical problems such as recurrent infections, growth failure, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, or antibiotic usage.
* Assess stability of gene correction by serial measurement of percent of nucleotide-converted alleles.

Exploratory Endpoints:

* Evaluate specificity by assessing for off-target edits at predicted sites with high-throughput sequencing of the 5 most common candidate off-target loci identified by a comprehensive in vitro screen, Circularization for High-throughput Analysis of Nuclease Genome-wide Effects by sequencing (CHANGE-seq-BE), in peripheral blood cells.
* Determine rate of random off-target edits WGS.

Participants will be randomized to receive either JCXH-108 or placebo.

description:
This Phase 1 study plans to enroll a total of 75 participants.

Three cohorts with two different dose levels will be explored and each cohort will enroll 25 participants. Participants in each cohort will be randomized (4:1) to receive either JCXH-108 (n=20) or placebo (normal saline, n=5). A low dose of JCXH-108 will be explored vs placebo in the 18-45 years of age group first. A high dose will be explored vs placebo in the 18-45 years and ≥ 60 years of age groups once safety data is reviewed for the Sentinel subjects in the low dose cohort. The dose level of JCXH-108 will depend on the time the participant joins the study. Each participant will receive a single dose of JCXH-108 administered intramuscularly (IM) on day 1.

abstract: Traditional adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (AD-MSCs) research has relied on unfractionated bulk populations, whose therapeutic efficacy is constrained by cellular heterogeneity, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and rapid postengraftment functional exhaustion, resulting in inconsistent outcomes and impeding clinical translation. This review systematically examines AD-MSC developmental origins, tissue niches, isolation and purification strategies, functional phenotypes, and biomanufacturing bottlenecks. It integrates preclinical and clinical evidence for AD-MSCs and their extracellular vesicles (EVs) in bone and cartilage regeneration, chronic cutaneous diseases, neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and other conditions. These therapies remodel injured microenvironments through immunometabolic reprogramming, antifibrotic signaling, angiogenesis, mitochondrial transfer, and paracrine regulation rather than direct tissue replacement. Major translational barriers include cellular heterogeneity, safety concerns, the transdifferentiation controversy, nonstandardized preconditioning, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and low cell retention after transplantation. We propose that clinical translation should be based on prospective isolation of functional subpopulations, coupled with tailored preconditioning, precision gene editing, three-dimensional biomaterials, EV engineering, and automated closed-system biomanufacturing. This framework aims to preserve potency, phenotypic stability, and paracrine function, transforming AD-MSCs and their bioactive derivatives from variable, unfractionated preparations into well-characterized, standardized, highly potent precision biologics. More broadly, it offers a mechanism-driven, function-defined, engineering-enabled, and clinically accessible roadmap for next-generation regenerative medicine.

abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.

abstract: Genetic engineering can transform bacteria (including Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and Yersinia) from naturally occurring microbes into programmable therapeutics. Unlike passive platforms, engineered bacteria can localize to defined biological niches, sense environmental cues, regulate programmed activity in situ, interact with host tissues in novel ways, and persist for controlled periods. These properties make bacteria versatile medicines but require genetic control of precision, safety, stability, and activity under clinical conditions. Major design layers include strain or "chassis" selection, attenuation and biocontainment, control of therapeutic activity, targeting and persistence, and genotype-to-phenotype stability during manufacturing and in vivo use. These features also create liabilities, including off-target behavior, unstable expression, and evolutionary loss of function under selection. Progress depends on safe, clinically translatable chassis with integrated, bounded, and durable behaviors. This review examines the genetic design principles and liabilities of bacteria-based therapeutics, approaches used to produce clinical and near-clinical candidates, and the emergence of programmed bacteria delivering complete gene editing systems to therapeutically relevant cells.

title: Genetic principles enabling the creation of bacteria-based therapeutics.

abstract: Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic RNA viruses, including filoviruses, henipaviruses and Rift Valley Fever virus (RVFV), pose a significant threat to human health. Due to their epidemic potential and high pathogenicity, these viruses are categorized as WHO priority pathogens, yet we still lack effective medical countermeasures (MCMs) against most of these dangerous pathogens, supporting that host-directed antivirals will be advantageous for broadly acting MCMs. Here we assessed the antiviral efficacy of SLR14, an immunomodulatory stem-loop RNA that activates RIG-I, for its activity against a panel of highly pathogenic viruses. SLR14 treatment provided broad-spectrum protection, markedly reducing infection with Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus, and Sudan virus in human primary monocyte-derived macrophages, and Nipah virus replication in iPSC-derived endothelial cells, whether administered prophylactically or therapeutically. In vivo, a single dose of SLR14 protected mice against lethal RVFV infection when administered prophylactically, and, notably, retained significant efficacy when administered up to two days post-infection. Therapeutic SLR14 administration also improved survival rates of EBOV-infected mice. Although EBOV infection and SLR14 treatment activated overlapping innate immune pathways in human macrophages, viral infection induced a nonprotective response, whereas SLR14 elicited a well-regulated, markedly stronger and protective interferon-stimulated and inflammatory gene signature while avoiding prolonged IFN gene upregulation. Our data identify SLR14 as a potent host-directed therapeutic with broad antiviral efficacy against some of the most lethal viral pathogens.

title: Immunomodulatory RIG-I Agonist SLR14 Confers Protection Against a Range of Highly Pathogenic Negative Sense RNA viruses.

abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8⁺ T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

title: Cullin-5 RING E3 ligase limits CD8⁺ T-cell persistence and effector responses during chronic antigen stimulation.

abstract: Parkinson disease is an ongoing neurodegenerative disorder, and both motor and non-motor symptoms are involved with the existing therapies having minimal effects on the disease but only symptom alleviation. The goal of this systematic literature review was to generalize up-to-date evidence on the next-generation pharmacological strategies to manage the symptoms and the disease in a patient with Parkinson disease. The review was based on PRISMA 2020 and included the analysis of peer-reviewed studies of human research published in 2015-2026 and retrieved in the key databases, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library. This included 30 eligible studies consisting of randomized studies, observational studies, and early clinical trials. The results show that, although dopaminergic treatment continues to play a central role in managing motor symptoms, new methods such as gene therapy, gene editing, stem cell-based regeneration, nanomedicine delivery systems, repurposed drugs, artificial intelligence-based precision medicine approaches have a good neuroprotective and disease-modifying potential. Nonetheless, the majority of new interventions are still in preclinical or first line clinical phase, with a defined subset of emerging gene-, cell-, and nanotechnology-based approaches evaluated only in animal or in-vitro models rather than in PD patients and associated with small sample size, invasive delivery, limited follow-up and lack of long-term safety information. In general, the review concludes by stating that there has been significant advancement in diversification of therapeutic targets and mechanisms, but rigorous large-scale biomarker-directed clinical trials are needed to translate these advances to effective and sustainable treatment of the Parkinson disease.

title: Next-generation pharmacological strategies for Parkinson's disease: a systematic literature review of symptom management and disease modification.

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation.

abstract: This review examines the expanding role of PARP inhibitors in cancer therapy, moving beyond the traditional model of single-strand break repair inhibition and BRCA-dependent synthetic lethality. We highlight emerging evidence that PARP inhibitors induce cytotoxicity through replication-associated DNA damage, including defects in Okazaki fragment maturation and replication gap accumulation. By integrating recent mechanistic insights with findings from CRISPR-based screens, we outline how disruptions in DNA replication and repair pathways define a broader BRCAness phenotype. We further emphasize the clinical implications of these discoveries, including novel combination strategies that extend the therapeutic applicability of PARP inhibitors beyond prevailing treatment regimens.

title: Widening the BRCAness therapeutic window for its synthetic lethality effects with PARP inhibitors.

abstract: Alternative splicing is a key regulatory mechanism known to be altered upon viral infection. These alterations can arise both from direct viral interference with the splicing machinery and from cellular responses such as activation of innate immunity. Here, we investigated splicing changes shared between dengue virus (DENV) infection and interferon (IFN) treatment in cultured cells, the latter serving as a model for virus-independent innate immune activation. Among the common events, we identified an increased production of non-coding mRNA isoforms from the CLK1 gene, which gives rise to a kinase that phosphorylates splicing factors including SR proteins and spliceosomal components. Consistent with this finding, IFN treatment led to a reduction in CLK1 protein levels. Using stable cell lines with CRISPR/dCas9-mediated modulation of CLK1 expression, we found that silencing CLK1 enhanced the induction of immune response genes, while its over-expression attenuated it. Inhibition of CLK1 kinase activity with the pharmacological inhibitor TG003 further potentiated IFN-induced gene expression and reduced DENV replication. Altogether, these results identify CLK1 as a proviral negative regulator of IFN-stimulated gene expression and suggest that its inhibition could enhance antiviral defenses and become a target for therapeutic strategies.

title: Targeting CLK1 by CRISPR tools and pharmacological inhibition modulates the innate immune response and dengue virus replication.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Drug-resistant tuberculosis is a significant global health issue caused by mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the infectious agent of the disease. WHO's End TB Strategy mandates drug susceptibility testing for rifampicin in all confirmed tuberculosis cases and fluoroquinolone testing for rifampicin-resistant cases.
OBJECTIVE: The review aims to analyse Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome mutations; Clinical factors linked to drug resistance. Major thematic findings: The mutant otsB1 trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase shows rifampicin resistance in hypoxic conditions. Pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 is vital for RNI resistance, host cell death, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth. Individuals with drug-susceptible tuberculosis showed higher plasma levels of inducible nitric oxide synthase. NO and iNOS expression can be influenced by factors other than mycobacterial infection. Activated macrophages convert L-arginine to NO via TNF-α and IFN-γ. Serum L-arginine levels were measured in individuals with pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and healthy controls. PPE51, PE15, and PE20 improve drug resistance by transporting metal ions and absorbing nutrients. In diagnosis, the CRISPR-guided mutagenic DNA polymerase identifies changes in drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Mycobacterium smegmatis, recognized for its rapid growth, and the slow-growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis were evaluated using CRISPR-guided DNA polymerase. Also, machine learning and whole-genome sequencing predicted isoniazid, Rifampicin, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis with 90% precision. The BDQ DILI network can offer valuable support on monitor the adverse events of the Anti-tuberculosis therapy.
CONCLUSION: Whole genome sequencing, tNGS, and deletion-targeted multiplex PCR effectively detect mutations. Studying PE/PPE genes offers a key chance to drug-resistant tuberculosis research and improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes.
